topics: Preface — purpose and audience: material developed for the CCRMA spectral-modeling course offered since 1984, aimed at beginning graduate students in computer music and engineering.

Preface — prerequisites and method: Fourier transforms, elementary digital signal processing, digital filtering, and linear systems support a computational treatment of spectral analysis, modeling, modification, and resynthesis.
Preface — Book Series Overview: dependency map placing this volume among related online books and showing which background texts support its advanced topics.

Introduction and Overview — spectral perception: the cochlea separates frequencies analogously to a prism, motivating Fourier-domain descriptions of timbre, source separation, formants, periodic signals in noise, speech consonants, and tonal music.
Introduction and Overview — Elementary Spectrum Analysis: finite records, the DFT, windowing, and the interpretation of magnitude spectra.
Introduction and Overview — Short-Time Fourier Transform and Time-Frequency Displays: repeated windowed transforms as the central analysis tool for nonstationary audio.
Introduction and Overview — Short-Time Analysis, Modification, and Resynthesis: spectral editing, overlap-add reconstruction, and the phase vocoder as the book's main processing arc.

Introduction and Overview — STFT Applications and Multirate Filter Banks: spectral modeling, time scaling, filter-bank views, polyphase structures, perceptual coding, and wavelets previewed for later chapters.
Chapter 2 — Fourier-transform taxonomy: DFT, DTFT, Fourier series, and continuous Fourier transform classified by finite/infinite and discrete/continuous time and frequency domains.
Chapter 2 — DTFT definition and interpretation: spectrum as inner products or projections onto complex sinusoids, with inverse synthesis over one 2π-periodic frequency interval.
Chapter 2 — continuous Fourier transform and inverse: transform pairs, convergence qualifications, and generalized-function treatment of idealized signals.
Chapter 2 — DTFT theorems: linearity, time reversal, conjugation and Fourier symmetry, shifts and linear phase, convolution, correlation, autocorrelation, and Parseval's power theorem.
Chapter 2 — multirate Fourier theorems: stretching by zero insertion, spectral repetition, downsampling and alias summation, antialias filtering, and rational L/M conversion.
Chapter 2 — differentiation and spectral roll-off: multiplication by time index corresponds to frequency differentiation; increasing endpoint smoothness accelerates asymptotic decay.
Chapter 2 — spectral interpolation: a finite record's DTFT is exactly interpolated from DFT samples by a periodic aliased-sinc kernel.

Chapter 2 — zero padding: denser sampling of the same underlying spectrum, FFT-friendly lengths, peak-display interpolation, zero-phase conventions, and prevention of time aliasing after spectral modification.
Chapter 3 — Rectangular Window: Dirichlet/asinc spectrum, narrow main lobe, fixed high sidelobes, Gibbs leakage, and the effect of increasing record length.
Chapter 3 — Generalized Hamming family: cosine taper as a sum of shifted rectangular-window spectra; Hann and Hamming endpoint, sidelobe, roll-off, and main-lobe tradeoffs.
Chapter 3 — MLT sine window: coding-gain optimum, minimum moment of inertia, transform coding, and time-domain alias cancellation with 50-percent overlap.
Chapter 3 — Blackman-Harris family and cos^P windows: multi-term cosine windows, shifted-spectrum implementation, and systematic endpoint-smoothness versus roll-off design.
Chapter 3 — Spectrum Analysis of an Oboe Tone: measured-record comparison under rectangular, Hamming, and Blackman windows, demonstrating leakage-limited weak-harmonic visibility.
Chapter 3 — preemphasis: approximately +6 dB/octave spectral flattening for voice and a practical leaky differentiator with a one-pole inverse.
Chapter 3 — Bartlett, Poisson, and Hann-Poisson windows: triangular convolution construction, exponential z-plane contraction, and monotone sidelobe-free decay for suitable Hann-Poisson parameters.
Chapter 3 — DPSS/Slepian window: maximization of energy concentration inside a prescribed main-lobe band via the principal eigenvector of a sampled-sinc Toeplitz matrix.
Chapter 3 — Kaiser window: modified-Bessel approximation to DPSS with a continuous beta parameter controlling time-bandwidth and sidelobe attenuation.
Chapter 3 — Dolph-Chebyshev window: minimax/equiripple sidelobe design, closed-form Chebyshev construction, length estimate, and endpoint-impulse risk.
Chapter 3 — Gaussian window: Fourier self-similarity, minimum second-moment time-bandwidth product, and quadratic log magnitude enabling accurate parabolic peak interpolation.
Chapter 3 — optimized windows: framing a window as a zero-passband lowpass FIR approximation, with perceptual, time-domain, monotonicity, and derivative constraints.
Chapter 3 — linear-programming window design: symmetric positive samples, normalized DC response, stopband bounds, minimax objective, and optional monotonicity or derivative regularization.
Chapter 4 — FIR-design framing: finite filters as approximations to desired frequency responses under explicit norms, constraints, transition widths, and perceptual priorities.
Chapter 4 — ideal lowpass filter: rectangular frequency response and its infinite, noncausal sinc impulse response.
Chapter 4 — lowpass specifications: passband ripple, stopband attenuation, transition bandwidth, dB-to-linear conversions, and why a nonzero transition band is indispensable.
Chapter 4 — naive least-squares truncation: exact time-domain truncation is L2-optimal by Parseval yet performs poorly when asked to approximate a discontinuous brick wall without transition freedom.
Chapter 4 — frequency-sampling FIR design: inverse DFT of sampled desired responses, intersample deviations, time aliasing, and verification with a heavily zero-padded FFT.

Chapter 4 — window method: multiply the ideal impulse response by a finite window; in frequency this convolves the desired response with the window transform and sets transition width by main-lobe width.
Chapter 4 — Kaiser bandpass example: empirical beta and length formulas, a 101-tap 20 kHz design, equal-transition-width limitation, and comparison with a Remez equiripple result.
Chapter 4 — Hilbert-transform design: analytic signals, positive-frequency retention, ±90-degree phase response, and ideal impulse response 1/(πt).

Chapter 4 — practical Hilbert transformer: half-sample centering avoids the singularity, symmetric transition bands force alternating zero taps, and a long frequency-sampled target is Kaiser-windowed to the final length.

Chapter 4 — generalized window method: smoothly interpolate an arbitrary desired response, choose or synthesize phase, inverse transform, verify energy concentration under the window, window, then compare achieved and desired spectra.

Chapter 4 — minimum-phase design: Hilbert-transform relation between log magnitude and phase, the cepstrum, causality, and reflection of unstable poles or nonminimum-phase zeros through the unit circle.
Chapter 4 — Lp optimal FIR design: weighted frequency-response error under L1, L2, and L∞ norms as a generally convex optimization in the coefficients.
Chapter 4 — Chebyshev/Parks-McClellan design: unique minimax weighted-error solution, equiripple alternation, efficient Remez exchange, and numerical convergence limits at high orders.

Chapter 4 — least-squares linear-phase design: even impulse-response symmetry reduces the response to a cosine basis; normal equations and the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse implement orthogonal projection.
Chapter 4 — Chebyshev design by linear programming: introduce a scalar error bound and minimize it subject to linear inequalities, trading Remez efficiency for more general constraints.

Chapter 4 — general and nonlinear-phase FIR design: complex desired spectra handled with real coefficients by stacking real and imaginary equations; examples include inverse, fractional-delay, polyphase, and minimum-phase filters.
Chapter 4 — convex and nonlinear optimization: second-order cone methods and general optimization tools extend FIR design to quadratic constraints and perceptually driven objectives.

Chapter 5, Spectrum Analysis of Sinusoids: why short-time sinusoidal peaks are compact models for tonal audio, additive synthesis, model calibration, pitch estimation, source grouping, selected-source modification, and noise reduction.

§5.1, Spectrum of a Sinusoid: amplitude, phase, radian/Hz frequency, decomposition of a real sinusoid into positive- and negative-frequency complex exponentials, analytic signal, and the impulse-pair Fourier spectrum.
§5.2, Spectrum of a Sampled Complex Sinusoid: normalized radian frequency, discrete-time complex exponentials, and the periodic DTFT impulse representation.

§5.3, Spectrum of a Windowed Sinusoid: finite observation as time-domain windowing, rectangular versus tapered windows, zero-centered and causal forms, and the linear phase introduced by shifting a window.

§5.4, Effect of Windowing: multiplication/convolution duality, the sinusoid becoming a shifted and scaled window transform, main-lobe smearing, sidelobe leakage, and competing definitions of an optimal analysis window.
§5.4.1, Frequency Resolution: main-lobe width as the resolution control, the rectangular window as the narrowest-main-lobe choice, and dependence on window length.

§5.4.1 examples, Two In-Phase Cosines and Phase-Quadrature Sine/Cosine: controlled window-length experiments showing apparent resolution, amplitude/frequency bias, and sensitivity to relative phase when peaks overlap.
§5.5, Resolving Sinusoids: zero-crossing, moment, and engineering definitions of main-lobe width; window-family bandwidth tables; sufficient peak-separation rules; and difference-frequency cycles.
§5.5.1, Other Definitions of Main-Lobe Width: smooth windows without zero crossings and the filter-design interpretation of passband, transition band, stopband, and sidelobe specification.
§5.5.2, Simple Sufficient Condition for Peak Resolution: separating shifted window main lobes, M >= K fs/|f2-f1|, effective width K, and empirical sharper constants K-star.

§5.5.3, Periodic Signals: harmonic spacing, driven versus freely vibrating sources, the rule M >= KP for period-P signals, and equal effective lengths across rectangular, Hamming, Blackman, and Blackman-Harris windows.

§5.5.4, Tighter Bounds for Minimum Window Length: orthogonal, stationary-point, sidelobe-matched, and full-main-lobe separation rules, with the stationary-point spacing as a near-optimal practical criterion.
§5.6, Sinusoidal Peak Interpolation: zero-padding plus quadratic interpolation as QIFFT, perceptual error tolerance, and comparison with ideal spectral interpolation.

§5.6.1, Quadratic Interpolation of Spectral Peaks: three-bin parabolic fitting in dB magnitude, closed-form peak location/height/curvature, exactness for an ideal Gaussian-window transform, phase interpolation, and Matlab implementation.
§5.6.2, Bias of Parabolic Peak Interpolation: systematic model-mismatch error, unbiased bin-centered and half-bin cases, and hybrid zero-padding/interpolation design.
§5.7, Optimal Peak-Finding in the Spectrum: the QIFFT procedure, zero-padding factors for inaudible bias, low- versus high-frequency perceptual bounds, and Matlab design calculations.

§5.7, Least-Squares Sinusoidal Parameter Estimation: complex sinusoid plus white-noise model, nonlinear/nonconvex frequency fitting, projection-based amplitude and phase estimates, and DTFT-magnitude frequency search.

§5.7, Maximum-Likelihood Sinusoid Estimation: Gaussian likelihood, equivalence with least squares, multiple well-resolved sinusoids, nonlinear optimization for overlapping peaks, prewhitening for colored noise, and the general deterministic-mean result.
Chapter 6, Spectrum Analysis of Noise: stationary stochastic-process viewpoint, autocorrelation and PSD estimation, biased/unbiased conventions, averaging, and practical audio examples.

§6.1, Introduction to Noise: tape-hiss denoising and spectral-modeling synthesis as motivating uses; finite sequences cannot reveal randomness without a model; stationary noise is treated as filtered white noise.

§§6.2–6.3, Spectral Characteristics and White Noise: random spectral phase, phase removal through magnitude-squared spectra, whiteness as lack of sample correlation rather than a particular amplitude distribution, and empirical whiteness tests.
§6.4, Sample Autocorrelation: unbiased lag-product averaging, finite-support indexing, sample variance at zero lag, convergence to the true autocorrelation, and the impulse test for white noise.
§6.5, Sample Power Spectral Density: PSD as the DTFT of autocorrelation, total area as variance, real/even symmetry, and the flat spectrum of white noise.

§§6.6–6.9, Biased, Smoothed, and Cyclic Autocorrelation/PSD Estimates: Bartlett lag weighting, asinc-squared spectral smoothing, FFT implementation with zero padding, optional mean/trend removal, and the need for ensemble/time averaging.
§6.10, Why an Impulse Is Not White Noise: deterministic frequency-flat impulse versus stationary white noise, plus a blockwise stationarity test that separates them.
§6.11, The Periodogram: normalized squared-magnitude DTFT/FFT, Bartlett-smoothed PSD interpretation, asymptotic expected value, and inconsistency caused by variance comparable to the mean.

§§6.12–6.13, Welch's Method: frame-wise periodograms, time averaging, autocorrelation counterpart, resolution–stability compromise, overlap/COLA-compatible windows, block count, and Matlab implementation.
§6.14, Filtered White Noise: colored, pink, and brown noise; autocorrelation and PSD determined by the shaping filter; moving-average and 1/f synthesis/analysis examples.
§6.15, Processing Gain: coherent sinusoidal versus noncoherent noise addition, N-fold DFT-bin SNR gain, 3 dB per doubled transform length, and the necessity of quoting SNR bandwidth.
§6.16, The Panning Problem: amplitude-preserving versus power-preserving stereo gains, frequency-dependent interaural coherence, and why equal-power panning is the practical default.
Chapter 7, Time-Frequency Displays: STFT as a sequence of local spectra, classic speech/audio spectrograms, and perceptually motivated loudness displays.
§7.1, The Short-Time Fourier Transform: goals of perceptual display and model measurement, pitch versus fundamental frequency, mathematical definition, window hop, and constant-overlap-add condition.
§7.1, Practical STFT Computation: time-normalized frames, zero-centered windows, zero-padding, FFT buffer rotation, optional phase restoration, and the window/frame/FFT/hop parameter roles.

§7.1, Dual Interpretations and Time-Frequency Distribution: overlap-add frame sequence versus downsampled uniform filter bank, and rectangular time-frequency resolution cells bounded by time-bandwidth tradeoffs.
§7.2, Classic Spectrograms: log-magnitude STFT intensity, time/frequency oversampling, parameter tuning, cochlear analogy, synthesis-model matching, and a measured speech example.
§7.2.1, Spectrogram of Speech: 20 ms Hamming analysis, fourfold spectral interpolation, phoneme localization, harmonic resolution, pitch/formant tracking, and interpretation of vocal-tract formants.

§7.3, Audio Spectrograms and Auditory Filter Banks: limits of a uniform-resolution STFT, nonuniform constant-Q/wavelet/gammatone/gamma-chirp banks, excitation patterns, critical-band sampling, and specific loudness.

§7.3.2, Loudness Spectrogram: multiresolution STFT, level- and frequency-dependent auditory interpolation kernels, nonuniform spectral resampling, excitation patterns, compressive specific loudness, and temporal loudness smoothing.

§7.3.3 examples: measured-speech MRSTFT, excitation pattern, auditory filter shapes, specific loudness, four-way display comparison, and instantaneous/short-term/long-term loudness in sones and phons.
Chapter 7 Summary: STFT-based path from classic spectrogram through auditory resampling and nonlinear compression to loudness-versus-time/frequency displays.
Chapter 8, Overlap-Add STFT Processing: the STFT as a hopping sequence of windowed spectra used to implement FIR filtering and frame-varying spectral modification.
Chapter 8.1, Convolution of Short Signals: cyclic versus acyclic convolution, zero padding, the N_x+N_h-1 output-length rule, time-domain aliasing, and FFT-versus-direct cost.
Chapter 8.1.4, Audio FIR Filters: perceptually short filters can still be hundreds of taps, making FFT convolution important in audio.
Chapter 8.2, Convolving with Long Signals: block decomposition, overlap-add convolution, output-block ringing, and the efficient rectangular-window case M=N-L+1.
Chapter 8.2.1, COLA: partition-of-unity reconstruction, practical Hamming/Hann/Blackman cases, periodic versus symmetric endpoints, and numerical verification of window/hop pairs.
Chapter 8.3, Dual of COLA: Poisson summation, frame-rate harmonics, weak versus strong COLA, and time/frequency Nyquist duality.
Chapter 8.4-8.6, Overlap-save and WOLA: discarding aliased samples, time-varying filter taps, synthesis windows, power-complementary window pairs, and root windows.
Chapter 9, Filter-Bank View of the STFT: OLA as time-ordered spectra versus FBS as frequency-ordered narrowband time signals.
Chapter 9.2-9.3, STFT filter bank: demodulation to baseband, lowpass filtering by the flipped window, remodulation, channel summation, and the DFT filter-bank special case.
Chapter 9.4-9.7, Reconstruction constraints: Nyquist(N) windows, COLA/Nyquist Fourier duality, Portnoff windows longer than the DFT, and deliberate time aliasing before the FFT.
Chapter 9.8, Downsampled STFT banks: hop size as per-channel decimation, anti-aliasing limits, alias cancellation, and why modification-robust hop sizes are smaller than maximal COLA hop sizes.
Chapter 9.9-9.10, Modified STFTs: fixed and time-varying FBS filters, OLA/FBS dual limits, and the trade between filter length and coefficient-variation bandwidth.
Chapter 10.1, Fundamental-frequency estimation: peak-spacing histograms, least-squares harmonic fits, pre-emphasis/masking, and harmonic-comb refinement.
Chapter 10.2-10.3, Cross-synthesis and spectral envelopes: carrier flattening, modulator-envelope transfer, cepstral liftering, and linear-prediction envelopes.
Chapter 10.3.2, Linear prediction: all-pole source-filter modeling, autocorrelation/covariance/Burg methods, peak-sensitive ratio error, stability, and model-order selection.
Chapter 10.4, Spectral modeling synthesis: additive partial tracks, sinusoidal peak measurement and tracking, deterministic/stochastic decomposition, and residual-noise envelopes.
Chapter 10.4.4, Sines+Noise+Transients: explicit transient regions, multiresolution maps, Bark-band noise envelopes, phase matching, and a continuous transientness control.
Chapter 10.5, Time-scale modification: STFT resampling over time, phase continuation versus relative-phase preservation, transient handling, and SOLA-FS comparison.
Chapter 10.6, Chirplets: Gaussian-windowed linear chirps, complex-Gaussian transform pairs, quadratic log-magnitude/phase, and curvature-based chirp-rate estimation.
Chapter 10.7, FFT filter banks: grouping STFT bins into arbitrary bands, smaller per-band IFFTs, critically sampled channel signals, and nonuniform/constant-Q designs.

Chapter 10.7.4-10.7.10, Practical audio filter banks: channel-filter transition/stopband control, real-signal partitions, stopband-only aliasing, overlapping power-of-two IFFT bands, and quasi-octave designs.
Chapter 11.1-11.2, Multirate operations and polyphase decomposition: spectral images, alias sums, noble identities, and efficient filtering before decimation.
Chapter 11.3, Critically sampled PR banks: two-channel alias/filtering cancellation, Haar, QMF, CQF, orthogonal and biorthogonal choices.
Chapter 11.4-11.5, General polyphase PR and paraunitary banks: analysis/synthesis polyphase matrices, inversion conditions, paraconjugation, losslessness, and power complementarity.

Chapter 11.9, Wavelet filter banks: Hilbert-space bases, overcomplete STFT frames, continuous/discrete wavelets, dyadic constant-Q banks, and generalized STFTs.

key_results: Chapter 2, Fourier-transform taxonomy: the four standard transform cases are DFT (finite/discrete time and frequency), DTFT (infinite discrete time, continuous periodic frequency), Fourier series (finite periodic continuous time, discrete frequency), and FT (infinite continuous time and frequency).
Chapter 2, DTFT: X(ω)=Σ_n x(n)e^{-jωn}, with x(n)=(1/2π)∫_{-π}^{π}X(ω)e^{jωn}dω; the spectrum is 2π-periodic.

Chapter 2, Fourier interpretation: each transform value is an inner product with a complex sinusoid, so analysis measures projection and inverse transformation synthesizes the signal from those components.
Chapter 2, symmetry: for real x, X(-ω)=conj(X(ω)); consequently magnitude and real part are even, while phase and imaginary part are odd modulo phase wrapping.
Chapter 2, shift theorem: x(n-l) transforms to e^{-jωl}X(ω); delay changes only phase, adding a linear phase slope of -l.
Chapter 2, convolution and correlation: (x*y) transforms to XY, while cross-correlation transforms to conj(X)Y; autocorrelation therefore transforms to |X|².
Chapter 2, Parseval/power theorem: the time-domain inner product equals the corresponding normalized frequency-domain inner product, preserving energy across transform domains.
Chapter 2, stretch/repeat theorem: inserting L-1 zeros between time samples produces L spectral repetitions; str_L(x) corresponds to rpt_L(X).
Chapter 2, downsampling theorem: retaining every Mth sample gives Y(ω)=(1/M)Σ_{k=0}^{M-1}X(ω/M+2πk/M); overlap among these copies is aliasing, prevented by limiting the input to |ω|<π/M.
Chapter 2, rational resampling: conversion by L/M is conceptually upsample by L, lowpass-filter the spectral images/aliases, then downsample by M.

Chapter 2, Riemann roll-off: if a window has n derivatives with the appropriate bounded-variation smoothness, its transform decays asymptotically as O(1/ω^{n+1}); endpoint smoothness buys approximately another 6 dB/octave per order.

Chapter 2, exact spectral interpolation: the DFT samples uniquely specify the DTFT of a finite record through periodic aliased-sinc interpolation; computing an IFFT, zero-padding in time, and taking a longer FFT performs uniform interpolation exactly.
Chapter 2, zero-padding limitation: padding adds no signal information and cannot improve true resolution; it samples existing lobes more densely for display and peak estimation.
Chapter 2, zero-phase padding: a zero-centered sequence must place nonnegative times at the buffer start and negative times at the end; padding belongs between them, not after the apparent sequence.

Chapter 3, rectangular window: an M-sample zero-phase rectangle has W(ω)=sin(Mω/2)/sin(ω/2), first sidelobe near -13 dB, approximately 6 dB/octave sidelobe decay, and main-lobe width 4π/M between first zeros.
Chapter 3, window-length effect: increasing M narrows the rectangular main lobe but does not lower its relative sidelobes; leakage level is controlled by window shape, not record length alone.

Chapter 3, Hann window: the α=1/2 generalized-Hamming member has endpoint value and slope zero, first sidelobe about -31.5 dB, approximately 18 dB/octave decay, and a main lobe twice as wide as the rectangular window's.
Chapter 3, Hamming window: α=25/46≈0.54 nearly minimizes peak sidelobe in its two-term cosine family, reaching about -42.76 dB; nonzero endpoints restore a 6 dB/octave asymptotic roll-off.

Chapter 3, MLT sine window: when applied in both analysis and synthesis, its square is a Hann window; time-domain alias cancellation permits 50-percent overlap in transform coders such as MP3 and AAC.

Chapter 3, Blackman-Harris family: an L-term cosine window transforms into a sum of 2L-1 shifted rectangular spectra, permitting efficient frequency-domain smoothing; the classic Blackman has about -58 dB peak sidelobes and 18 dB/octave decay.

Chapter 3, oboe comparison: at the chosen durations, a rectangular window obscures upper harmonics with leakage, Hamming reveals more, and Blackman clearly reveals the harmonic series because its lower sidelobes accommodate the recording's large spectral dynamic range.
Chapter 3, Bartlett window: a triangle is the convolution of two rectangles, so its transform is a squared asinc; its main lobe is twice the rectangular width and its first sidelobe is about -26 dB.
Chapter 3, Poisson window: multiplying an impulse response by an exponential taper contracts its z-plane transfer function radially, H_P(z)=H(z/r), a useful system-identification interpretation.

Chapter 3, Hann-Poisson window: for decay parameter α at least about 2, magnitude decreases monotonically away from its peak, providing a nominally sidelobe-free objective useful for hill-climbing peak searches.

Chapter 3, DPSS optimum: the discrete prolate spheroidal sequence maximizes the ratio of spectral energy in a chosen main-lobe interval to total energy and is the principal eigenvector of a sampled-sinc symmetric Toeplitz matrix.

Chapter 3, Kaiser approximation: beta=0 yields the rectangle; with α=β/π, the first-null estimate is (2π/M)sqrt(1+α²), and widening by roughly one rectangular main-lobe unit buys about 25 dB of sidelobe reduction.
Chapter 3, Dolph-Chebyshev optimum: for fixed main-lobe width it minimizes maximum sidelobe level, producing equiripple sidelobes; an approximate length is 1+(2/ω_c)acosh(1/r).

Chapter 3, Gaussian uncertainty: the Gaussian transforms to a Gaussian and achieves the minimum second-moment time-bandwidth product σ_tσ_ω=1; its log magnitude is exactly quadratic, motivating parabolic interpolation.

Chapter 3, window optimization: minimax stopband design with linear equality/inequality constraints is a linear program; monotonicity and L1 or L∞ derivative penalties can suppress undesirable time- or frequency-domain behavior.
Chapter 4, ideal lowpass: H(ω)=1 inside |ω|≤ω_c and zero outside has h(n)=sin(ω_cn)/(πn)=2f_c sinc(2f_cn), which is infinite and noncausal.

Chapter 4, transition-band necessity: truncating a brick-wall ideal response to 30 or 71 taps yields only roughly 10 dB of stopband rejection and corner ringing, whereas granting a finite transition band enables a 71-tap Remez design beyond 60 dB; a useful scale is transition width at least about 4π/L.

Chapter 4, frequency-sampling warning: the inverse DFT exactly matches desired samples but may deviate badly between them and suffer time aliasing, so every design must be inspected with a much denser, zero-padded response grid.

Chapter 4, window method duality: time-domain multiplication by w convolves the ideal frequency response with W; achievable transition width is governed by the window main lobe and narrow passbands cannot be smaller than roughly half that width.

Chapter 4, Kaiser sizing: the empirical length law M≈(A-8)/(2.285Δω), paired with the standard piecewise beta estimate, converts attenuation and transition-width specifications into a practical first design.

Chapter 4, equal-transition limitation: a single window shape imposes essentially the same transition width at every band edge; unequal requested widths are therefore rounded toward the most demanding edge unless a more general optimization is used.

Chapter 4, analytic signal: the ideal Hilbert transformer has H(ω)=j for negative frequencies, 0 at DC, and -j for positive frequencies; x_a=x+jH{x} cancels negative frequencies and doubles positive ones.

Chapter 4, Hilbert kernel: the continuous ideal impulse response is h(t)=1/(πt), noncausal and singular at zero; a practical even-length design centers zero between samples, introducing a half-sample delay that must also be applied to the real path.
Chapter 4, Hilbert design economy: choosing transition bands symmetrically around one-quarter the sample rate forces every other impulse-response coefficient to zero, halving the filtering work.

Chapter 4, generalized window design: a fast noniterative sequence—smooth desired response, inverse FFT, verify concentration, window, FFT, compare—scales to thousands of taps and is suitable for interactive or adaptive frequency-response shaping.

Chapter 4, minimum phase from magnitude: for a minimum-phase H=Ge^{jΘ}, Θ is the Hilbert transform of ln G; equivalently the log spectrum is analytic and its inverse transform, the cepstrum, is causal.

Chapter 4, cepstral minimum-phase conversion: add each negative-time cepstral coefficient to its positive-time counterpart and zero the negative side; this reflects unstable poles and nonminimum-phase zeros inside the unit circle.
Chapter 4, Lp formulation: minimize ||W(ω_k)[H(ω_k)-D(ω_k)]||_p over FIR coefficients; p=2 gives least squares and p=∞ gives minimax/Chebyshev design, normally within a convex problem.

Chapter 4, Chebyshev optimum: the unique minimax solution has alternating equal-magnitude weighted-error extrema; Remez/Parks-McClellan converges monotonically in exact arithmetic but commonly becomes numerically unreliable beyond a few hundred taps.

Chapter 4, least-squares geometry: for an even zero-phase FIR, H is a cosine-series matrix A times the independent coefficients; the solution satisfies A^TAh=A^Td and is the orthogonal projection A A†d of the target onto A's column space.
Chapter 4, numerical least squares: solve the overdetermined system directly with a stable linear solver rather than explicitly forming the pseudoinverse or normal-equation inverse.

Chapter 4, complex-response fitting: a nonlinear-phase target with real coefficients is reduced to a real least-squares problem by vertically stacking Re(A), Im(A) and the corresponding real and imaginary desired-response samples.

Chapter 4, method tradeoff: window/frequency-sampling methods are fast, robust at very high orders, and naturally drooping; Chebyshev methods use taps more efficiently with equiripple bands and tighter transitions but cost much more design time and can fail numerically.
§5.1: A real sinusoid A cos(omega0 t+phi) is the sum of conjugate complex exponentials with coefficients (A/2)exp(±j phi); its Fourier spectrum is a conjugate pair of impulses at ±omega0.
§5.3: shifting a length-M zero-centered window by (M-1)/2 samples to make it causal multiplies its transform by exp(-j omega(M-1)/2), introducing linear phase without changing magnitude.

§5.4: windowing a complex sinusoid produces S_R(omega)=2pi W(omega-omega0); therefore every measured sinusoidal peak is exactly the analysis-window transform shifted to the tone frequency and scaled by its complex amplitude.

§5.4: the window-transform main lobe limits separation of nearby frequencies, while sidelobes limit detection of weak tones near strong tones; these are distinct failure modes requiring different window choices.

§5.4.1 examples: two sinusoids separated by Delta omega can look spuriously resolved or displaced when their window-transform lobes overlap; only the two-difference-cycle rectangular case is insensitive to the tested relative phase.
§5.5: for a length-M rectangular window, side-lobe spacing is Omega_M=2pi/M and zero-to-zero main-lobe width is 2 Omega_M=4pi/M, equivalently 2 fs/M hertz.
§5.5.2: a simple sufficient resolution requirement for a window whose main lobe spans K bins is M >= K fs/|f2-f1|—the window must span at least K cycles of the minimum difference frequency.

§5.5.2/Table 5.2: sharper empirically verified K-star values for accurate FFT-peak measurement are approximately 1.44 rectangular, 2.22 Hamming, 2.36 Hann, and 2.02 Blackman, substantially below full zero-to-zero separation.
§5.5.3: for a periodic signal with P samples per fundamental period, resolving harmonics is assured by M >= KP; differing physical window lengths can thus share the same effective resolution length.

§5.5.4: placing one peak at the first stationary point of the other's main lobe makes both derivatives vanish at the true peaks, removing first-order peak-location bias and closely approximating optimal minimum spacing.

§5.5 Summary: as a broad design rule, an analysis window should see at least about 1.5 cycles of the minimum difference frequency; tapered windows have shorter effective durations than their sample counts suggest.
§5.6.1: for dB magnitudes alpha, beta, gamma at bins -1,0,1 around a peak, the parabolic offset is p=(1/2)(alpha-gamma)/(alpha-2 beta+gamma), and the peak height is beta-(1/4)(alpha-gamma)p.

§5.6.1: quadratic interpolation is exact for an ideal Gaussian window on a dB scale because its log-magnitude transform is a parabola; other windows are locally quadratic only as a Taylor approximation.

§5.6.2: parabolic peak estimates are unbiased when the true peak is exactly on a DFT bin or halfway between bins, but generally biased elsewhere; zero-padding provides exact bandlimited spectral interpolation and controls that bias.

§5.7/Table 5.3: for peak-frequency bias below 0.1% of fs/M, minimum zero-padding factors are about 4.1 rectangular, 2.4 generalized Hamming, and 1.8 Blackman; 0.1% frequency error is normally inaudible in audio.

§5.7 low-frequency bounds/Table 5.4: below roughly 1 kHz, a fixed 1 Hz error criterion better matches frequency JND data; Blackman needs no zero padding below 125 Hz and generalized Hamming none below 62.5 Hz for one-period windows.

§5.7, amplitude/phase estimation: with known frequency, the optimal complex least-squares estimate is the normalized projection Ahat exp(j phihat)=(1/N) DTFT_omega0{x}; amplitude and phase are its magnitude and argument.
§5.7, frequency estimation: the least-squares estimate of an unknown single-sinusoid frequency maximizes |DTFT_omega{x}|; evaluating the complex projection there supplies its amplitude and phase.

§5.7, likelihood: for a deterministic sinusoid in independent zero-mean Gaussian white noise, maximizing likelihood is identical to minimizing squared residual error, so the DTFT-peak estimator is both LS and ML.

§5.7, multiple sinusoids: independent interpolated peak finding approximates ML only when peaks are well resolved and sidelobe overlap is negligible; overlapping lobes require joint nonlinear optimization over amplitudes, phases, and frequencies.

§5.7, nonwhite noise/general result: colored noise should be prewhitened before applying the white-noise estimator; more generally, ML equals LS for any deterministic mean model plus zero-mean Gaussian white noise.
Chapter 6 introduction: the PSD is the DTFT of autocorrelation, S_x(omega)=DTFT{r_x}; for zero-mean signals its integral over normalized frequency equals r_x(0), the variance/average power.
§6.4: the unbiased sample autocorrelation uses 1/(N-|l|) times the sum of available lag products; at l=0 it is sample variance, and for white noise it converges to sigma^2 delta(l).

§§6.6–6.7: ordinary finite-signal autocorrelation is the unbiased sample autocorrelation multiplied by a Bartlett window; correspondingly, its squared-magnitude spectrum is the sample PSD smoothed by an asinc-squared kernel.

§6.9: an acyclic sample autocorrelation can be computed by zero-padding an M-sample signal to FFT size N>=2M-1, taking |FFT|^2, inverse transforming, and optionally dividing out the Bartlett lag weights.
§6.10: an impulse has a flat spectrum and impulse autocorrelation but is not white noise because it is not stationary; blockwise autocorrelations expose one nonzero block followed by zero blocks.

§6.11: the periodogram P=(1/M)|DTFT{x_w}|^2 has the correct asymptotic expected value but standard deviation comparable to its mean, so increasing record length alone does not yield a stable per-band noise-level estimate.
§6.12: Welch's estimate is the arithmetic mean of K windowed-frame periodograms, Shat_x^W(omega_k)=(1/K)sum_m P_xm,M(omega_k); averaging, not merely transforming, creates statistical stability.
§6.12.2: with N_x samples, a practical default balances resolution and stability by choosing frame length M and frame count K both approximately sqrt(N_x).

§6.13: nonrectangular Welch windows should overlap so their shifts sum to a constant; typical hops are (M-1)/2 for generalized Hamming windows and about M/3 for Blackman, with K=floor((N_x-M)/R)+1 frames.
§6.14: if x=h*v and v is white with variance sigma_v^2, then r_x(l)=sigma_v^2(h star h)(l) and S_x(omega)=sigma_v^2|H(omega)|^2; all correlation/color is embodied by the shaping filter.

§6.14.1: an eight-tap moving-average process has triangular autocorrelation 8-|l| for |l|<8 and PSD sin^2(4 omega)/sin^2(omega/2), illustrating exact time/frequency dual descriptions of colored noise.

§6.14.2: ideal pink-noise PSD is proportional to 1/f and requires amplitude response proportional to 1/sqrt(f), which no finite-order rational filter realizes exactly; stable IIR approximation can nevertheless be perceptually exact.

§6.15: an N-point DFT gives N-fold processing gain for a bin-centered sinusoid in white noise: expected signal power grows as N^2 A^2 while per-bin noise grows as N sigma_v^2, adding 3 dB SNR per doubled N.
§6.15: frequency-domain SNR is meaningless without a bandwidth; narrowing a filter around a zero-bandwidth deterministic component repeatedly removes noise while retaining the signal.

§6.16: coherent equal speaker signals preserve amplitude at center with gains (1/2,1/2), while uncorrelated signals preserve power with (1/sqrt(2),1/sqrt(2)); real stereo panning commonly chooses the latter.
§7.1.1: X_m(omega)=sum_n x(n)w(n-mR)exp(-j omega n); if shifted windows satisfy sum_m w(n-mR)=1, then sum_m X_m(omega)=X(omega), the whole-signal DTFT.

§7.1.1: rectangular windows are COLA at hop M, while Bartlett and generalized Hamming windows are COLA at M/2 with proper endpoints; COLA is essential for artifact-free reconstruction but can be relaxed for display-only analysis.

§7.1.2: with window length M and FFT length N>=M, frequency sampling is information-preserving because the windowed frame is time limited; zero-padding factor N/M is the ideal spectral interpolation factor.

§7.1.3: the STFT is simultaneously a time sequence of local Fourier transforms and a bank of frequency-shifted lowpass filters whose outputs are downsampled by hop R; the window is each channel's anti-aliasing impulse response.
§7.1.4: an STFT tiles time-frequency space with uniform rectangular resolution cells; window length and type set the cell aspect ratio and area, bounded below by a time-bandwidth uncertainty product.

§7.2: a classic spectrogram is a log-magnitude intensity plot of the STFT; M controls frequency resolution, window type controls sidelobes, N controls frequency interpolation, and R controls time-axis sampling.

§7.2.1: a 20 ms speech window is short enough to localize most frames within one phoneme yet long enough to contain at least two periods of a 100 Hz voiced fundamental, balancing harmonic resolution with tracking of pitch and formants.

§7.3.1: an auditory filter bank is a nonuniform frequency sampler; each auditory-filter response acts as a frequency-dependent interpolation kernel, and its output power defines the excitation pattern.
§7.3.2: a loudness spectrogram pipeline combines multiresolution STFT, auditory-filter resampling, and a level/frequency-dependent compressive nonlinearity to produce specific loudness per ERB.
§7.3.2: instantaneous loudness is the sum of specific loudness across frequency; short- and long-term loudness apply asymmetric temporal smoothing that rises quickly and decays more slowly.

§7.3.3: spectral smoothing by auditory kernels shortens effective time windows, so the maximum safe hop must be re-evaluated from the combined window or widest auditory-filter bandwidth rather than inherited blindly from the original MRSTFT.

Ch. 8 opening and Sec. 8.2: if the analysis window is COLA at hop R, sum_m w(n-mR)=1, then the original signal is recovered by summing its windowed frames; multiplying each frame spectrum by H_m produces a linear time-varying OLA processor.

Secs. 8.1.2-8.1.3: an acyclic convolution of lengths N_x and N_h has at most N_x+N_h-1 nonzero samples; an FFT implementation must use N at least that large or wrapped terms produce time-domain aliasing.

Sec. 8.1.4: direct convolution is O(N^2) while FFT convolution is O(N log N), but the crossover is implementation- and hardware-dependent; long audio FIRs strongly favor FFTs on a CPU, whereas GPUs can push the crossover to thousands of taps.

Secs. 8.2.1-8.2.6: long-signal convolution can use nonoverlapping rectangular input blocks with M=N-L+1 and R=M; their filtered outputs overlap by L-1 samples and sum to the exact acyclic convolution.

Sec. 8.2.1: library window names do not by themselves guarantee COLA. Endpoint conventions matter: a symmetric Hamming window can leave periodic impulses in the overlap sum, while its appropriate periodic/end-corrected variant reconstructs exactly.

Secs. 8.3.1-8.3.2: Poisson summation gives sum_m w(n-mR)=(1/R)sum_k W(2pi k/R)e^(j2pi kn/R). Hence w is COLA(R) iff W vanishes at every nonzero frame-rate harmonic; exact bandlimiting to |omega|<pi/R is stronger and modification-robust but impossible for finite-duration windows.

Secs. 8.4 and 8.6: overlap-save uses an N-point FFT without zero padding, discards L-1 aliased output samples, and advances R=N-L+1; WOLA instead applies a synthesis window f and requires sum_m w(n-mR)f(n-mR)=1.

Sec. 8.6.2: with identical analysis and synthesis windows, WOLA requires shifted squared windows to sum to a constant. Taking the square root of any nonnegative OLA window constructs a valid WOLA window, explaining the root-Hann/MLT sine window.

Secs. 8.5.1-8.5.2: in time-varying OLA, each desired FIR tap sequence is convolved with the analysis window, so the window lowpass-filters tap variation; zero padding limits frame-filter length while the window limits time-variation bandwidth.

Secs. 9.1-9.3: regrouping the STFT sum shows each bin as a channel signal: demodulate x by exp(-j omega_k n), lowpass-filter by the flipped analysis window, then sample in time. The window transform is therefore the channel-filter shape.

Secs. 9.4-9.6: OLA and FBS reconstruction conditions are Fourier duals: w in COLA(R) iff W is Nyquist(2pi/R), while w is Nyquist(N) iff W is COLA(2pi/N). The DFT bank with a rectangular window reconstructs by remodulation and summation.

Sec. 9.7: Portnoff windows w(n)=w_0(n)sinc(n/N) are Nyquist(N) even when longer than the FFT; time-aliasing the windowed frame to N samples sharpens channel filters but makes reconstruction more fragile under spectral modification.

Secs. 9.8.3-9.8.5: for an L-term Blackman-Harris-family window of length M, suppressing main-lobe aliasing requires roughly R<=M/(2L), whereas maximal weak-COLA hopping is M/L. The latter reconstructs unmodified signals by alias cancellation but is less robust to modifications.

Sec. 9.9.1: fixed FBS gains synthesize y=x*[flip(w)h], so the window time-limits the desired impulse response and smooths its frequency response; OLA instead leaves h intact up to a scale when padding and COLA conditions hold.

Sec. 9.9.3: FBS permits arbitrarily fast frame-to-frame coefficient changes but limits filter length to the window, whereas OLA permits longer filters through padding but bandlimits tap variation. These are another Fourier-dual pair.

Secs. 10.1-10.1.2: a practical F0 estimate combines the mode of spectral-peak spacings with a least-squares fit f_k=kF0, then may refine F0 by maximizing a harmonic-comb product (or log sum) over interpolated magnitude samples.

Secs. 10.3.1-10.3.2: cepstral envelopes lowpass-window the real cepstrum of log|X|; LP envelopes arise from whitening with a monic prediction-error filter A(z), yielding approximately sigma_e/|A(e^jomega)|.

Sec. 10.3.2.1: LP minimizes an integrated spectral ratio error |Y/Y_hat|^2, making underestimation of spectral peaks costly; it therefore tends to overestimate peaks and compensate with equal-area log-magnitude valley underestimation.

Secs. 10.4.1-10.4.4: efficient audio models should assign evolving peaks to sinusoidal tracks, dense residual energy to filtered noise, and abrupt events to an explicit transient representation; phase is most crucial around transients.

Secs. 10.5.2-10.5.4: STFT time scaling interpolates magnitudes across frame time, but phase continuation and preservation of inter-bin relative phase conflict. Favor continuation for stationary tones and relative phase near transient peaks; WOLA crossfades residual frame-boundary error.

Secs. 10.6.1-10.6.4: a Gaussian-windowed chirp has parabolic log magnitude and unwrapped phase in frequency. Their curvatures c_m and c_p give chirp-rate estimate beta_hat=alpha_hat[c_p]/[c_m], with best estimates near high-SNR peaks.

Secs. 10.7.2-10.7.4: if a filter-bank band spans N_k adjacent FFT bins, an N_k-point IFFT yields its critically downsampled time signal; exact reconstruction follows by FFTing each channel frame and reassembling the original spectral bins, provided the underlying STFT is PR.

Secs. 10.7.5-10.7.10: practical modified banks should embed each desired passband plus both transitions in an overlapping power-of-two IFFT band. Downsampling then aliases only stopband energy, whose bound is controlled by the chosen prototype window attenuation.

Secs. 11.1-11.2: upsampling by N inserts N-1 zeros and creates N spectral images; downsampling selects every Nth sample and aliases N expanded spectral copies. Polyphase/noble-identity forms move filtering to the low-rate side and reduce work by about N.

Secs. 11.3.1-11.3.7: two-channel PR needs both the X(-z) alias term to cancel and the X(z) transfer to reduce to gain and delay. CQF constraints derive all four filters from one lowpass prototype and give FIR, orthogonal, exact PR at the cost of linear phase except for Haar.

Secs. 11.4.4-11.4.5: for an N-channel bank with R dividing N, R(z)E(z)=c z^-K I is sufficient for reconstruction x_hat(n)=c(N/R)x(n-N+1-K); the fully general PR condition differs only by channel permutation and at most one extra sample of channel delay.

Secs. 11.5.1-11.5.3: a paraunitary polyphase matrix is unitary on the unit circle and is inverted by its paraconjugate. FIR analysis then implies FIR time-reversed synthesis filters, channel power complementarity, and energy preservation.

Sec. 11.7.3: MP3 combines a 32-channel 512-tap PQMF bank with 6- or 18-band lapped transforms (192 bands for transients, 576 for steady tones); AAC instead switches a single MDCT bank between 128 and 1024 bands.

Secs. 11.8 and 11.9: oversampling is generally preferred when signals will be analyzed or modified; critical sampling is primarily a compression requirement. STFT bases become overcomplete when windows overlap, while wavelet/dyadic banks trade uniform resolution for constant-Q time-frequency tiling.
Appendix A, Frequency and Time: ω is rad/s, f is Hz with ω=2πf; T is the sample interval, fs=1/T, and tn=nT.
Appendix A, Signal/Fourier Notation: x∈C^N maps by the N-point DFT to X∈C^N; pointwise spectral multiplication is denoted XY and implemented as elementwise multiplication.
Appendix B, Differentiation: dx/dt transforms to jωX(ω), while -jtx(t) transforms to dX/dω.
Appendix B, Scaling: x(t/α) transforms to |α|X(αω); stretching time squeezes frequency and scales amplitude.
Appendix B, Shift and Modulation: x(t−τ) transforms to e^{-jωτ}X(ω), while x(t)e^{jνt} transforms to X(ω−ν).
Appendix B, Convolution/Power: time convolution transforms to spectral multiplication, and the time-domain inner product equals the properly normalized spectral inner product.
Appendix B, Impulse: the Dirac impulse is a generalized function characterized by unit area and the sifting property; it is the limit of any unit-area pulse shrinking to zero width.
Appendix B, Rect/sinc pair: a width-τ rectangular pulse transforms to τ sinc(fτ), and τ sinc(τf) converges distributionally to δ(f) as τ grows.
Appendix B, impulse trains: the normalized shah is self-Fourier; an impulse train spaced P seconds transforms to an impulse train spaced 1/P Hz with areas scaled by 1/P.
Appendix B, Poisson summation: periodic aliasing of w(t) with period R equals the inverse Fourier series formed from samples W(k/R)/R, making spectral sampling and time aliasing dual.
Appendix B, continuous sampling: multiplying x(t) by a T-spaced impulse train produces fs-scaled spectral replicas X(f−kfs); bandlimiting below fs/2 prevents overlap.
Appendix B, uncertainty: with duration and bandwidth defined as normalized second moments, Δt·Δω≥1/2, with equality only for a Gaussian.
Appendix B, time-limited bound: if x(t)=0 outside an interval of duration Δt, then Δt·Δω≥π under the appendix's second-moment bandwidth definition.
Appendix B, no upper uncertainty bound: an allpass filter can preserve bandwidth while extending duration arbitrarily.

Appendix B, Riemann lemma: if derivatives through order n have bounded variation, W(ω)=O(1/ω^{n+1}); practically, n smooth derivatives imply about -6(n+1) dB/octave roll-off until discrete-time aliasing flattens the envelope near Nyquist.
Appendix C, sample mean: for a stationary process, the N-sample average is an unbiased estimator of the true mean.
Appendix C, sample variance: division by N is unbiased when the true mean is known; replacing it by the sample mean requires division by N−1.
Appendix C, correlation spectra: DTFT{rxy} is the cross-PSD, DTFT{rx} is the PSD, and a real process has real-even autocorrelation and PSD.
Appendix C, white noise: whiteness requires zero correlation at nonzero lags, not a particular amplitude distribution; its autocorrelation is σ²δ(m) and its PSD is flat.
Appendix C, independence: independent zero-mean samples are uncorrelated; for jointly Gaussian variables, uncorrelatedness also implies independence.
Appendix C, averaging gain: the variance of an M-sample mean of uncorrelated samples is σ²/M.
Appendix C, variance-estimator variance: for zero-mean Gaussian white noise, Var(sample variance)=2σ⁴/M, again falling as 1/M.
Appendix D, Gaussian transform: (1/(σ√(2π)))e^{-t²/(2σ²)} transforms to e^{-ω²/[2(1/σ)²]}; narrowing in one domain widens reciprocally in the other.
Appendix D, closure: products and convolutions of Gaussians remain Gaussian; the product variance is the reciprocal-sum combination σ1²σ2²/(σ1²+σ2²).
Appendix D, complex Gaussian integral: for Re(p)>0, ∫e^{-pt²}dt=√(π/p), and a complex shift does not change the integral.
Appendix D, complex Gaussian transform: e^{-pt²} transforms to √(π/p)e^{-ω²/(4p)} for Re(p)>0, covering Gaussian-windowed chirps.

Appendix D, Gaussian fitting: taking a logarithm converts a Gaussian peak to a parabola; weighted least squares should weight inverse noise variance, with data-amplitude weighting reported as useful in practice.
Appendix D, central-limit mechanism: repeated convolution raises a smooth-tipped characteristic function approximately (1−αω²)^N≈e^{-Nαω²}, explaining convergence toward a Gaussian.

Appendix D, entropy: h(p)=E[log2(1/p(x))] is the average ideal code length; a fair random bit has entropy 1 bit, while probabilities 1/4 and 3/4 yield 0.81128 bits and about 19 percent compressibility.

Appendix D, maximum entropy: the uniform distribution maximizes entropy on a fixed finite interval, the exponential maximizes it on [0,∞) for fixed mean, and the Gaussian maximizes it on the real line for fixed mean and variance.
Appendix D, Gaussian moments: odd central moments vanish and even moments are (n−1)!!σ^n, giving m4=3σ⁴, m6=15σ⁶, and m8=105σ⁸.
Appendix D, moment theorem: E{x^n}=(1/j^n)d^nΦ/dω^n evaluated at zero, where Φ is the characteristic function.
Appendix E, Bark scale: 24 published critical bands span 0 to 15.5 kHz; one Bark is one critical bandwidth, and the inverse mapping should be optimized so errors are measured perceptually in Barks.
Appendix E, bilinear map: z=(ζ+ρ)/(1+ρζ) maps the unit circle to itself, fixes DC and Nyquist, has inverse coefficient -ρ, and preserves filter order because the substitution is first order.

Appendix E, Bark fit quality: at 31 kHz, optimal Chebyshev, least-squares, and weighted equation-error maps are nearly identical; L2 is within 0.04 Bark of L∞, below typical critical-band measurement uncertainty.

Appendix E, Bark errors: at 31 kHz, peak mapping error is about 0.64 Bark for Chebyshev and 0.67 Bark for least squares; relative bandwidth-mapping error is about 18–20 percent when optimized for slope.

Appendix E, perceptual significance: measured auditory-filter bandwidths vary widely across listeners, so a 20 percent worst-case mapping error may be detectable by expert listeners but lies inside empirical population variation.
Appendix E, Bark coefficient shortcut: with fs in kHz, rho≈1.0674√[(2/π)atan(0.06583fs)]−0.1916 closely approximates the optimal Chebyshev map and generally adds under 0.1 Bark peak error.

Appendix E, filter-design result: prewarping a desired response to Bark, fitting there, and unwarping yields a same-order filter that allocates approximation accuracy more evenly per critical band; the 12th-order example fits below 4 kHz much better than an unwarped fit.
Appendix E, ERB formulas: ERB(f)=0.108f+24.7 Hz and ERBS(f)=21.4log10(0.00437f+1); ERB approaches about 11 percent of center frequency at high frequencies and about 25 Hz at low frequencies.

Appendix E, ERB limitation: at 31 kHz a first-order map has about 1.9 Bark peak error and over 60 percent peak relative-bandwidth error—roughly three times the Bark case—because it cannot stretch low frequencies enough.
Appendix F, DPSS code: build the sampled-sinc Toeplitz matrix, take the eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue, and normalize its peak to obtain the maximum-concentration window.
Appendix F, quadratic interpolation: three uniform samples around a maximum determine offset p=(y+1−y−1)/[2(2y0−y+1−y−1)], peak height, and curvature.

Appendix F, STFT reconstruction test: a properly normalized COLA Hamming window with 50 percent hop reconstructs the chirp example to relative L2 error around 8×10^-16 for both odd and even window lengths.

Appendix F, fundamental estimation: after interpolating spectral peaks, assign harmonic numbers and solve a one-parameter least-squares regression; the test estimates 440 Hz as 439.99 Hz with all harmonics and 437.50 Hz after notching out the fundamental.

Appendix G, vocoder architecture: Dudley's original system analyzed ten bands over 250–3000 Hz, sent their amplitude envelopes plus F0/voicing, and resynthesized with buzz or hiss through matching filters.

Appendix G, phase vocoder: adding complex channel phase removes explicit pitch tracking because phase modulation fine-tunes a sinusoid within its band, but good compression still assumes no more than one sinusoid per channel.

Appendix G, IFFT synthesis: writing whole window-transform main lobes rather than isolated FFT bins creates time-shaped sinusoidal envelopes; chirp-rate-indexed main lobes extend this to within-frame frequency sweeps.
Appendix G, FM spectra: kth sideband amplitude is proportional to Jk(beta); increasing modulation index moves power into more sidebands and perceptually brightens the tone.

Appendix G, FM voice compression: three FM carrier/modulator pairs can approximate three vowel formant groups using six oscillators, versus as many as about 200 additive oscillators for a 100 Hz voice extending to 20 kHz.

Appendix G, envelope compression: slowly varying tonal amplitude/frequency envelopes historically reached roughly 100:1 compression; critical downsampling of N filter-bank channels by N returns one parameter sample per input sample overall.

Appendix G, modern sinusoidal modeling: replacing the uniform vocoder bank by an STFT peak-adaptive sparse bank avoids empty channels and tracks inharmonic partials; it can be understood as a pruned phase vocoder.

Appendix G, sines+noise+transients: sinusoids compactly represent tonal components, filtered white noise represents the steady residual, and explicit transient segments preserve attacks without hundreds of partials.

Appendix G, perceptual sparsity: a tones/noises/attacks model achieved AAC-comparable quality around 32 kbps while remaining amenable to time and frequency transformations; the text reports over 90 percent of typical audio information can often be removed inaudibly.

Appendix H, hop-size criterion: COLA is conservative and guarantees equal weighting, while modified-STFT alias control instead requires the folding frequency fs/(2R) to exceed the window cutoff; resulting overlaps are 50 percent rectangular, 75 percent Hann/Hamming, and about 83 percent Blackman.
Appendix H, buffer rule: a zero-centered odd window stores zero and positive times first, negative times at the buffer end, and all zero padding in the middle.

Appendix H, peak accuracy: brute-force bin selection needs roughly 1000× padding for 0.1-percent peak-position accuracy, while three-bin parabolic interpolation reaches that target with about 5× padding for a rectangular window.
Appendix H, log-domain interpolation: fitting the top three samples in dB gives empirical frequency estimates about twice as accurate as fitting linear magnitude; p=0.5(α−γ)/(α−2β+γ).

Appendix H, track assignment: each prior track claims the nearest current peak within a frequency-dependent limit; conflicts go to the closer track recursively, unmatched tracks ramp down, and unused peaks start new zero-ramped tracks.

Appendix H, legal modifications: spectral multiplication is safe if zero padding accommodates the corresponding time convolution; inverse-transform the modification and monitor buffer-midpoint energy to expose time-alias risk.

Appendix H, sinusoidal synthesis: amplitude is linearly interpolated, while endpoint phase and frequency constraints require a cubic phase polynomial with the cycle count chosen for maximum smoothness.
Appendix H, reverse analysis: reversing a sound lets the stable decay establish important tracks before the noisy attack, preventing the fixed oscillator pool from being consumed by transient peaks.

Appendix H, perceptual result: phase-free synthesis can sound equivalent in some cases despite a visibly different waveform, but phase becomes crucial for speech, modifications, and inaudible splicing of sampled attacks to modeled steady states.

Appendix H, extreme reduction: PARSHL reportedly preserved intelligible speech using only the three strongest sinusoidal components, motivating a hypothesis of higher-level spectral-feature dominance beyond critical-band masking.
pedagogy: The book uses a spiral, duality-driven approach to computational audio DSP. It progresses from Fourier review, windows, and FIR design through sinusoid/noise estimation and time-frequency displays, then reframes STFT processing as overlap-add, filter-bank, multirate, wavelet, and application machinery before supplying mathematical, psychoacoustic, historical, and executable-code appendices. The recurring lesson loop is physical or auditory motivation, explicit derivation, implementation in MATLAB/Octave, heavily zero-padded visual or listening inspection, controlled comparison, deliberate failure, and repair. The same operator is repeatedly viewed in time, frequency, statistical, geometric, perceptual, and filter-bank forms, making equivalence—not formula memorization—the central habit. Worked scripts, parameter sweeps, measured audio, numerical tables, and embedded exercises serve as laboratories; conventional end-of-chapter problem sets are less central in the live chapters. A reusable course sequence is to derive a condition, violate it, diagnose the artifact, and repair the window, hop, padding, estimator, or polyphase structure. Learners should enter with complex arithmetic, calculus, linear systems, convolution, DTFT/DFT/FFT, and basic FIR filtering; later material adds z transforms, linear algebra, probability/Gaussian models, programming fluency, and elementary auditory perception. Particular strengths are exact implementation conventions, candid warnings about numerical and indexing traps, quantitative links between DSP and hearing, and project-ready paths from analysis to resynthesis.
