gems: Introduction, Motivation: the ear is compared to a prism because the cochlea spatially separates sound by frequency; the analogy immediately turns Fourier analysis from abstract decomposition into a model of hearing.
Introduction, Motivation: Hubble's discovery of galactic redshift is used as a vivid example of extracting physical meaning from displaced spectral lines.

Chapter 2, Fourier Transform as Projection: transform analysis is described as 'measuring how much' of each complex sinusoid is present, a reusable bridge from vector inner products to continuous spectra.

Chapter 2, Zero Padding Example: a 21-point Hamming window is shown with no padding, 2× padding, and dense references; two samples per lobe look improved, but 10× still visibly misses details while 100× and 1000× become indistinguishable.

Chapter 2, Zero Padding: the text distinguishes five legitimate uses—radix-friendly FFT length, smooth displays, peak interpolation, room for spectral modifications, and avoiding time aliasing—from the false claim of added resolution.
Chapter 3, Generalized Hamming: the familiar Hamming constant is not arbitrary; 25/46≈0.54 nearly reaches the family's Chebyshev optimum, with -42.76 dB versus the theoretical -43.19 dB minimum.

Chapter 3, Hamming Use Case: approximately 40 dB sidelobe suppression is tied to 'one-percent accurate' systems and roughly 8-bit telephone-codec quality, translating a window plot into an engineering tolerance.

Chapter 3, MLT Sine Window: applying the sine window twice squares it into Hann, and time-domain alias cancellation makes the resulting 50-percent overlap a practical coding construction used in MP3/AAC.

Chapter 3, Oboe Figures 3.16-3.18: two periods with a rectangular window, four with Hamming, and six with Blackman form a memorable controlled experiment in which only the lowest-sidelobe choice clearly reveals all upper harmonics.

Chapter 3, Voice Preemphasis: the approximately -6 dB/octave spectral tilt of voiced sound motivates a +6 dB/octave differentiating prefilter; the practical leaky form 1-0.95z^-1 retains an easy one-pole inverse.
Chapter 3, Hann-Poisson: a window can deliberately trade the usual lobe pattern for a monotone magnitude slope, turning spectral peak finding into a friendlier hill-climbing or convex-search problem.
Chapter 3, Kaiser Rule: increasing the main-lobe width by about one rectangular-window unit buys roughly 25 dB of sidelobe reduction, a compact mental estimate for beta/time-bandwidth tradeoffs.

Chapter 3, Dolph-Chebyshev Warning: the mathematically optimal equiripple sidelobes may create conspicuous impulses at the window endpoints, translating a frequency-domain optimum into audible pre/post echoes.

Chapter 3, Gaussian Peak Fitting: because Gaussian magnitude is quadratic in dB, three-point parabolic interpolation is exact for an ideal Gaussian lobe and often improves real spectral peak estimates.

Chapter 4, Bad Ideal Lowpass: a 71-tap truncated sinc still achieves only about 10 dB stopband rejection when no transition is allowed, whereas the same length exceeds 60 dB once a 0.5π-to-0.6π transition is specified.

Chapter 4, Kaiser Bandpass: a requested 20 kHz design with unequal transitions exposes a structural limitation—window designs want every transition to have the same main-lobe width—so one edge must be renegotiated.

Chapter 4, Hilbert Design: placing the 1/(πt) singularity halfway between samples simultaneously avoids infinity and produces the half-sample delay that an analytic-signal implementation must match in its real branch.
Chapter 4, Hilbert Symmetry: centering equal transition bands around fs/4 forces every other tap to zero, turning a symmetry observation into a factor-of-two computational saving.

Chapter 4, Kaiser versus Remez Hilbert Filter: the window design scales to thousands of taps and is almost instantaneous but wastes coefficients on passband overdesign and stopband droop; Remez roughly halves the transition width but takes orders of magnitude longer and fails near this 257-tap scale.

Chapter 4, Minimum Phase via Cepstrum: the recipe 'fold negative quefrencies onto positive ones, then zero the negative side' provides an implementable counterpart to the abstract statement that log magnitude and phase are Hilbert-transform pairs.

Chapter 4, Least-Squares Geometry: an overdetermined filter design becomes the literal orthogonal shadow of the desired response on the realizable cosine-basis subspace, making the normal equations visually inevitable.

Chapter 4, Optimization Choice: the chapter repeatedly shows that the norm is the design—L2 spreads error, L∞ controls the worst ripple, while added time-domain or derivative constraints encode artifact risks that a frequency-only optimum misses.

Sinusoidal models are called 'unreasonably effective' for tonal sound: the ear weights short-time spectral peaks so strongly that a sparse set of tracked peak parameters supports synthesis, calibration, pitch detection, source grouping, and tape-hiss rejection. [Chapter 5 introduction]

The same two tones can look resolved with a half difference-frequency cycle when placed in phase quadrature, yet the apparent peaks sit at the wrong frequencies. The example turns 'two bumps' from a visual judgment into a warning about estimator bias. [§5.4.1, Figs. 5.8–5.9]

Smith's memorable resolution unit is not FFT bins but cycles of the difference frequency: a window generally needs to see about 1.5 cycles, while full-main-lobe separation gives a conservative window-specific K-cycle rule. [§§5.5.2–5.5 Summary]

A 300-sample Blackman window, 200-sample Hamming window, and 100-sample rectangular window can all have roughly the same effective two-period resolving length; the discarded edge weight is made visible as lost effective duration. [§5.5.3, Fig. 5.13]

The stationary-point separation rule explains resolution through derivatives: put each peak over a stationary point of the other lobe and neither peak sits on a slope, eliminating first-order frequency bias. [§5.5.4, Fig. 5.14(b)]

Three adjacent dB bins are enough for a closed-form frequency and amplitude correction, and the method is exactly right for the conceptual Gaussian window because its log spectrum is already a parabola. [§5.6.1, Fig. 5.15]

The source quantifies 'perceptually exact' rather than leaving it rhetorical: 0.1% tuning error is generally inaudible, and Blackman needs only 1.8x zero padding for that bound, versus 4.1x rectangular. [§5.7, Table 5.3]

Low-frequency pitch acuity changes the engineering specification itself: below about 1 kHz, a fixed 1 Hz bound is more appropriate than a percentage, and some tapered windows need no zero padding at the lowest tested frequencies. [§5.7, Table 5.4]

QIFFT is not presented as a clever hack: orthogonal projection and Gaussian likelihood lead back to the same DTFT peak, making modest zero-padding plus parabolic interpolation a fast approximation to the actual LS/ML estimator. [§§5.6–5.7]

A finite list of random-looking numbers cannot prove randomness. Smith discloses that his eight-number example came from Matlab only after using it to insist that every noise analysis is ultimately a model fitted to data. [§6.1.2 What Is Noise?]

An impulse and white noise both contain every frequency equally, but only the noise is stationary. Splitting the record into blocks makes the distinction immediate: one impulse block followed by zeros can never look statistically comparable. [§6.10]

The periodogram has the right expected value yet the wrong temperament: its standard deviation is comparable to its mean. Welch averaging is therefore not cosmetic smoothing but the operation that turns random band values into a usable noise-level estimate. [§§6.11–6.12]

Pink-noise synthesis is a productive impossibility: no finite rational filter exactly realizes 1/sqrt(f) amplitude response, yet a short stable IIR approximation can be perceptually exact and then verified against the -3 dB/octave law. [§§6.14.2–6.14.3]

Processing gain is pictured as a coordinate change: sinusoidal energy piles into one DFT coordinate while noise stays spread everywhere, yielding N-fold SNR gain and 3 dB per doubled transform length. [§6.15]

The stereo-center gain has two correct answers. Coherent low frequencies want one-half per speaker; decorrelated energy wants one over square-root two. The standard equal-power pan law is a concession to frequency and listener geometry. [§6.16]

Smith separates pitch from fundamental frequency: when partials are stretched, perceived pitch may be a compromise frequency that is not physically present, while fundamental-frequency estimation remains a model-measurement problem. [§7.1]

COLA is treated with appropriate severity: violating it can create processing artifacts, but for a display-only spectrogram the same violation merely weights some time samples less, so 'nothing disastrous happens.' [§7.1.1]

The 20 ms speech window earns its canonical status with two simultaneous facts: it usually stays within one phoneme and still spans two periods of a 100 Hz voice, balancing event tracking against harmonic separation. [§7.2.1, Fig. 7.2]

The loudness-spectrogram sequence makes perception an inspectable algorithm: multiple FFT resolutions become ERB-spaced excitation, then compression becomes specific loudness, all applied to exactly the same speech utterance. [§7.3.3, Figs. 7.4–7.8]

The excitation-pattern plot reveals only four or five voiced harmonics but sharp pitch pulses at higher ERBs, while formants become clearer around 25 ERBs—a concrete demonstration that an auditory representation reorganizes, not merely smooths, spectral evidence. [§7.3.3, Fig. 7.5]

Sec. 8.1.4: the ear's nominal 10 ms integration time below 500 Hz becomes about 500 taps at 50 kHz, a memorable bridge from psychoacoustics to why ‘instantaneous’ audio FIRs still need FFT convolution.

Sec. 8.2.1: the default symmetric Hamming window leaves an impulse at every frame boundary under nominal 50% overlap; changing the endpoint convention repairs perfect reconstruction and makes COLA a testable engineering condition rather than a slogan.

Secs. 8.3.1-8.3.2: Poisson summation turns a window-overlap ripple into a short Fourier series whose coefficients are samples of W at frame-rate harmonics—the cleanest explanation in the shard of why exact reconstruction can coexist with channel aliasing.
Sec. 8.4: overlap-save's bookkeeping is unusually compact: use N input samples, accept L-1 corrupted outputs, retain R=N-L+1, and carry those L-1 input samples into the next frame.
Sec. 8.6.2: ‘take the square root of a good OLA window’ converts amplitude complementarity into power complementarity and immediately derives the root-Hann/MLT sine window used in coding.

Sec. 9.3.1: the ten-channel chirp experiment progressively swaps rectangular for Hamming windows and real for analytic chirps, separating leakage, channel overlap, and positive/negative-frequency beating in one reproducible sequence.
Secs. 9.8.3-9.8.5: the rule R_max=M/(2L) versus R_COLA=M/L for Blackman-Harris-family windows crisply separates ‘reconstructs when untouched’ from ‘survives modification.’

Secs. 9.8.5.2-9.8.5.3: a 33-sample periodic Hamming window at R=16 matches Poisson-summation prediction to roughly 10^-15, while a 33-sample Kaiser beta=8 window at R=6 gives about 58 dB stopband rejection—small laboratory-ready validations of theory.

Sec. 10.1.2: the harmonic-comb objective uses a small epsilon as insurance against a missing partial annihilating the product; the text also insists that optimized comb lines be overlaid on the actual spectrum to catch octave errors.
Sec. 10.3.3: a synthetic /ah/ vowel with formants at 700, 1220, and 2600 Hz lets students compare the true envelope against cepstral smoothing and an exact order-six LP model on known ground truth.

Sec. 10.4: Smith's ‘top ten percent spectral peak analyzer’ description of hearing motivates why a sparse sinusoidal model works remarkably well for tonal audio yet becomes wasteful for noise and transients.

Sec. 10.4.4: the model does not force a binary transient label; a transientness value from 0 to 1 controls how rigidly a region translates under time scaling, connecting perceptual uncertainty to a continuous algorithmic control.

Sec. 10.5.3: phase-vocoder TSM is framed as an impossible two-goal problem—continue each sinusoid smoothly or preserve inter-bin phase and within-frame envelopes—then assigns the goals differently to stationary and transient regions.

Sec. 10.5.4: two tones 10 Hz apart near 400 Hz, analyzed with 45 ms frames and 11.25 ms hops, expose different 2x-stretch artifacts for phase continuation, phase locking, and SOLA-FS without needing a complicated musical signal.

Sec. 10.6.3: chirp rate falls directly out of the ratio of phase and log-magnitude curvature at a Gaussian spectral peak; the sign flip in phase curvature immediately distinguishes rising from falling chirps.

Secs. 10.7.9-10.7.10: the 256-point, 127-tap, 80 dB Dolph-Chebyshev octave-bank example shows how including both transition bands before each power-of-two IFFT changes dangerous transition-band aliasing into controlled stopband aliasing.

Secs. 11.1.3-11.2.5: commuting a decimator into an FIR diagram removes N-1 out of N needless output computations, then polyphase notation and the noble identities explain exactly why the fast form is equivalent.

Secs. 11.3.3-11.3.4: the Haar bank collapses analysis and synthesis to sum-and-difference operations and simultaneously appears as a two-point rectangular STFT, a QMF, an orthogonal bank, and a polyphase OLA processor.

Sec. 11.3.7: no nontrivial two-channel filter bank can be simultaneously FIR, orthogonal, linear phase, and exact PR; CQF keeps FIR+orthogonal, biorthogonal designs trade orthogonality for linear phase, and Haar is the exception.

Sec. 11.7.3: MP3's transient/steady switch yields 192 versus 576 hybrid subbands, while AAC's simpler 128/1024-band MDCT switch illustrates how time-frequency resolution choices became codec architecture.

Sec. 11.8.6: the text's pragmatic extreme is a sliding FFT with R=1 and frequency zero-padding: computationally extravagant, but free of channel aliasing and therefore a high-quality reference for aggressive nonlinear modification.

Secs. 11.9.3-11.9.8: the STFT's uniform tiling and a dyadic wavelet bank's constant-Q tiling are developed from the same normalized-basis viewpoint, making wavelets feel like a change of basis geometry rather than an unrelated topic.

Appendix B, Uncertainty Principle: an allpass filter gives the shortest possible proof that time-bandwidth product has no upper bound—it changes no magnitude bandwidth but can extend duration without limit.
Appendix B, Smoothness and Roll-Off: the impulse-to-step-to-ramp ladder turns each time integration into one extra factor 1/(jω), making the -6 dB/octave per smooth derivative rule almost visual.

Appendix C, Random Variables: two dice turn two discrete uniform distributions into a triangular distribution by convolution, connecting an elementary probability experiment directly to an essential DSP operation.

Appendix C, White Noise with Dice: one die and two dice generate different amplitude histograms, yet both sequences are white if rolls are independent—a sharp separation of spectrum from marginal distribution.

Appendix C, Stationarity: 20 ms is offered as a typical frequency-independent audio frame over which statistics can be treated as approximately stationary; multiresolution frames instead span several center-frequency periods.
Appendix C, Estimator Variance: averaging M independent observations cuts variance by M, while Gaussian variance estimation costs twice the normalized variance, 2σ⁴/M.

Appendix D, Infinite Flatness: e^{-1/t²} has every derivative zero at t=0 yet is nonzero nearby, a striking counterexample to the intuition that an all-order Taylor series must recover a smooth function.
Appendix D, Random Bits: moving from a fair bit to probabilities 1/4 and 3/4 lowers entropy from 1 to 0.81128 bits, making the abstract entropy integral a concrete 19-percent compression opportunity.
Appendix D, Why Gaussian: the tiny local approximation 1−αω², raised by repeated convolution to the Nth power, becomes e^{-Nαω²}; the bell curve emerges from a one-line Fourier-domain limit.
Appendix D, Binomial Link: the bottom row of Pascal's triangle tends to a sampled Gaussian, so high-order Lagrange interpolation tends toward Gaussian-windowed sinc interpolation.

Appendix E, Psychoacoustic Equivalence: least-squares Bark warping lies within 0.04 Bark of the minimax optimum, below typical critical-band experimental uncertainty, so a closed-form practical map is as meaningful as the formal optimum.

Appendix E, Listener Variability: auditory-filter bandwidths around 2 kHz ranged roughly 230–410 Hz in one cohort and -33 to +65 percent in another, grounding a 20-percent mapping error in actual human variation.
Appendix E, Same-Order Perceptual Design: a first-order allpass warp lets a 12th-order filter spend accuracy per Bark and then unwarp while remaining 12th order.
Appendix E, Bark versus ERB: the same elegant first-order map is excellent for Bark but roughly three times worse for ERB, because ERB continues narrowing at low frequencies while Bark levels off.

Appendix F, Machine-Precision STFT: the short test program achieves roughly 8×10^-16 relative reconstruction error, giving learners a concrete pass/fail target for zero-phase indexing and COLA normalization.
Appendix F, Missing Fundamental: the harmonic-regression estimator returns 439.99 Hz for a 440 Hz tone and still returns 437.50 Hz after the 440 Hz component itself is removed.

Appendix G, Bernoulli Debate: 18th-century resistance to sinusoidal superposition included what would now be called intermodulation distortion—an intuitive but misplaced physical objection that took modern convergence theory to settle.

Appendix G, Voder Performance: ten fingers controlled band gains, a foot pedal controlled pitch, a wrist bar selected buzz or hiss, and about a year of training was needed to perform intelligible speech.

Appendix G, Vocoder Compression: the original ten-band 250–3000 Hz analysis reduced speech to F0/voicing plus ten slowly changing envelopes, accepting an 'electrical accent' for a much smaller transmission bandwidth.

Appendix G, FM Brass: Risset's observation that brass spectra brighten with amplitude led Chowning to make FM index proportional to the amplitude envelope—a measured acoustic regularity translated into one control connection.
Appendix G, FM Voice: six oscillators arranged as three FM pairs can approximate three formants that brute-force additive synthesis might represent with roughly 200 oscillators.
Appendix G, Model Progression: phase vocoder to sparse sinusoids to sines+noise to sines+noise+transients is presented as a sequence of fixing empty channels, noisy residuals, and costly attacks.

Appendix G, Sparse Brain Hypothesis: the observation that most primary auditory-cortex neurons are silent most of the time is used to ask what higher-level sparse representation follows the cochlea's spectrogram.
Appendix H, Padding Economics: 0.1-percent peak precision would require about 1000× zero padding by bin selection alone, but only about 5× when followed by a three-bin parabolic fit.

Appendix H, dB Interpolation: the original authors found parabolic peak-frequency interpolation in dB about twice as accurate as interpolation in linear magnitude and explicitly leave the optimal magnitude compression as an open question.
Appendix H, Reverse the Sound: analyzing decay-to-attack lets stable piano partials claim the finite oscillator pool before the noisy onset, a wonderfully simple algorithmic use of time reversal.

Appendix H, Be Gentle in Frequency: the practical warning links abrupt spectral edits to long time-domain filters, insufficient padding, and audible time aliasing; inspecting the inverse FFT of the modification makes the risk measurable.

Appendix H, Phase and Perception: magnitude-only synthesis may sound similar while looking radically different, yet phase is decisive for speech, transformations, and seamless attachment of real attacks to modeled sustains.

Appendix H, Three-Sine Speech: intelligible speech reportedly survives reduction to only the three strongest sinusoidal components, motivating the analogy between spectral peaks and the outlines that let vision recognize an object.

Appendix H, Living Source Artifact: the full 1985 SAIL implementation preserves not just algorithms but design diary comments about competing track-allocation strategies, making it unusually valuable as engineering history.
